headline: Often called “fake English”, サラリーマン may be real English with a letter dropped.
めがね was “eye metal” first; the kanji came from Chinese later.
The kanji say “soil” and “produce”; the likely origin is a shrine's “small box”.
いなか began as “winaka”, and its kanji came from a Chinese word.
Brothers have two readings, and they come from two waves of Chinese.
Soy sauce is “thick paste + oil”, and its sound has smoothed from /ɕauju/ to /ɕoːju/.
Buckwheat noodles carry a word whose root may be a “corner” — or a “feather”.
A Japanese-made word, built from Chinese parts, to name the telephone.
“Friend” is built as “friends”: an old plural that took over the singular.
Hand + paper gives “letter” in Japanese, but the identical characters in Chinese are an unrelated false friend.
Japanese パン is Portuguese pão, and behind that, Latin pānis.
The spelling you know isn't the original, and the sources disagree about why it works.
新しい was once “aratashi”: two syllables swapped places about a thousand years ago.
“Stuck flesh”: nobody is sure why a verb for sticking names sliced fish.
The Japanese word for a part-time job is German.
A teacher is, literally, someone “born earlier”.
“Tomorrow” was originally “next morning”, and the kanji came afterwards.
It sounds like English “consent” but it is “concentric plug”, shortened.
“Go out” + “mouth”: an exit is a door with a voiced mouth.
“Thank you” started out meaning “hard to exist”, which is to say, rare.
Fruit is literally “tree's thing”, with a lost possessive hiding in the middle.
Typhoon is a borrowing that was later dressed in Chinese-looking kanji.
A tatami is, at heart, something you fold.
Delicious began as an honorific: “o-” + “ishii”.
ゆかた is the front half of a longer word, and the kanji say “bathing garment”.
Nobody knows where たのしい comes from, and all three theories have problems.
A kimono was once just “a wearing-thing”: any clothing at all.
A “self-rolling vehicle”, coined in Japan in 1870 for a tricycle.
A fire was once “the matter of fire”, a native phrase later re-read in Chinese sounds.
“Dream” began as “sleep-eye”: sight seen while asleep.
けしき was spelled another way first; 景 was swapped in for the sense.
